question: Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If I Have No RevOps Function Yet?
body:
## Direct Answer Yes, hiring a fractional CRO before you have a RevOps function can work — but only if you treat that CRO as the person who *builds* the RevOps foundation, not one who inherits it. Without clean data, defined process, and shared definitions, even a great revenue leader is flying blind, so the engagement must explicitly include standing up the operational layer in its first 90 days. The instinct to hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer when growth stalls is understandable: you want senior go-to-market leadership without a full-time executive salary. But a CRO's leverage comes from acting on trustworthy signal — pipeline coverage, conversion rates, forecast accuracy — and none of that signal exists yet if you have no RevOps function. This essay walks through when the sequence works, when it backfires, and how to structure the engagement so the CRO and the RevOps buildout reinforce each other instead of stalling on missing data. ## What does a fractional CRO actually do without a RevOps team underneath them? A fractional CRO is a part-time senior revenue leader — typically 1-3 days a week — who owns the whole go-to-market motion: sales, and often marketing and customer success alignment, forecasting, pricing, and the commercial strategy that ties them together. The "fractional" part means you're renting executive judgment and pattern recognition from someone who has scaled revenue orgs before, without committing to a $250K-plus base plus equity. That model has genuinely matured over the last few years, and the value proposition is real for companies between roughly $2M and $20M in revenue that have outgrown founder-led sales but can't yet justify a full C-suite hire. The problem is that a CRO's core deliverables — an accurate forecast, a diagnosis of where deals die, a comp plan that drives the right behavior — all depend on an operational substrate that RevOps normally provides. RevOps is the function that owns the CRM's data model, the definitions of a qualified lead and a closed-won deal, the reporting layer, the tech stack integrations, and the process documentation. When that function doesn't exist, the CRO faces a choice: either build it themselves (or direct its buildout), or make decisions on gut and anecdote. A seasoned fractional CRO knows this and will insist on building the foundation first. A weaker one will start "coaching the team" and issuing pipeline mandates against numbers nobody trusts — and you'll pay for motion without progress. For a deeper look at how these responsibilities split, see the breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-vs-revops-scope. ![Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If I Have No RevOps Function Yet — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl0372-b1.jpg) ## When does hiring the CRO first actually make sense? There's a real case for the CRO-first sequence, and it hinges on one question: do you have a *revenue leadership* gap or a *revenue operations* gap? If your founder is still personally closing every meaningful deal, if there's no coherent sales methodology, if reps are freelancing their own processes, and if nobody owns the number — that's a leadership vacuum. A fractional CRO fills it immediately and can direct the RevOps buildout as a subordinate workstream, hiring or contracting the ops talent to execute the plumbing they specify. In that scenario, hiring the CRO first is correct, because the CRO defines *what* the operational layer needs to measure and enforce. The sequence also makes sense when you're pre-Series A or bootstrapped and simply can't afford two senior hires. A fractional CRO who is genuinely operations-literate can wear both hats for a period — setting strategy in the morning and cleaning up the CRM's deal stages in the afternoon — until revenue justifies splitting the roles. The key qualifier is "operations-literate": you must screen specifically for a CRO who has personally built a RevOps function before, not one who has always inherited a mature one. Ask them to walk you through the last CRM migration or forecast-model rebuild they led. If they can't, they'll be as lost in your unstructured data as you are. More on scoping that first-90-days mandate lives at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-first-90-days. ![Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If I Have No RevOps Function Yet — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl0372-b2.jpg) ## When should you build RevOps first — or hire them together? The opposite sequence — RevOps first — is right when your leadership is actually competent but drowning. If a capable founder or VP of Sales knows exactly what they'd do with clean data but spends every week wrestling spreadsheets, chasing reps for CRM hygiene, and rebuilding the same board report by hand, the bottleneck is operational, not strategic. A fractional or even junior RevOps hire unblocks that person immediately and is far cheaper than a CRO. Spending CRO money to solve a RevOps problem is a common and expensive misdiagnosis. The strongest pattern for well-funded companies is hiring both roughly together but with the RevOps person landing a few weeks ahead to prepare the ground. This lets the RevOps hire complete the foundational data audit and instrument the pipeline before the CRO arrives, so the CRO's first month is spent on strategy against real numbers rather than on discovering that the numbers are garbage. The decision tree below maps the common situations to the right first move. ![Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If I Have No RevOps Function Yet — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl0372-b3.jpg) ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Growth has stalled or plateaued] --> B{Is there a clear
revenue leader owning
the number?} B -->|No leader / founder-led| C{Can you afford
two senior hires?} B -->|Yes, capable but drowning| D[Build RevOps first] C -->|No| E[Fractional CRO first —
ops-literate, builds
foundation in 90 days] C -->|Yes| F[Hire both; RevOps

The failure mode to avoid is hiring a CRO, giving them no operational support, and then blaming them six months later for a forecast that was never buildable on your data. ![Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If I Have No RevOps Function Yet — figure 4](/assets/qa/tl0372-b4.jpg) ## What should the fractional CRO's first 90 days look like when RevOps doesn't exist? If you do hire the CRO first, the engagement's success is almost entirely determined by whether the first 90 days are structured around *building* rather than *performing*. A CRO who spends month one running pipeline reviews and pep talks against untrustworthy data is burning your money. The first quarter should be a foundation sprint with roughly this shape. Weeks 1-4 are diagnosis and definitions. The CRO audits the current state: what tools you have, what data lives where, how deals actually move (versus how the CRM claims they do), and where the real conversion cliffs are. Critically, this phase produces *shared definitions* — what counts as an MQL, an SQL, an opportunity, a closed-won deal, and each pipeline stage's exit criteria. Nothing downstream works until these exist, because a forecast is just arithmetic on definitions everyone has agreed to. Weeks 5-8 are instrumentation: standing up (or fixing) the CRM data model, wiring the reporting so the pipeline is visible without manual spreadsheet surgery, and hiring or contracting the RevOps execution talent to own it going forward. Weeks 9-12 are the first real operating cadence — a forecast the CRO will actually stake their name on, a diagnosed set of two or three high-leverage fixes, and a comp or process change to test. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Fractional CRO participant R as RevOps (hired/contracted) participant T as Sales Team participant D as Data/CRM C->>D: Weeks 1-4 audit state + set definitions C->>T: Interview reps on real deal flow C->>R: Weeks 5-8 spec the operational layer R->>D: Rebuild CRM model + reporting C->>T: Weeks 9-12 install operating cadence R->>C: Deliver trustworthy forecast signal C->>C: Diagnose top 3 fixes + comp change ``` Notice that RevOps talent gets brought in *during* the CRO engagement, not before it. This is the practical answer to the ordering question: the CRO front-loads the definitions and the target operating model, then hands the execution to a dedicated ops person or contractor. That division keeps the expensive CRO focused on judgment while the cheaper RevOps resource handles the labor-intensive plumbing. A fuller template for structuring this handoff is at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-foundation-checklist. ## How do you structure the engagement and measure whether it's working? Because you're hiring a fractional CRO precisely when you lack the internal instrumentation to evaluate them, you have to define success *contractually and behaviorally* at the outset, before the data exists to measure it. Set foundation-oriented milestones for the first quarter rather than pure revenue targets — you can't hold anyone to a bookings number that depends on infrastructure they're still building. Reasonable 90-day deliverables include: documented and adopted stage definitions, a working pipeline dashboard that leadership trusts, a forecast method with a stated accuracy expectation, a RevOps hire or contractor onboarded, and a prioritized list of go-to-market fixes with owners. Structurally, protect yourself on a few fronts. Insist on a defined weekly commitment in writing (fractional engagements blur easily), a clear reporting line — the CRO should report to the CEO/founder, not be buried under a VP — and explicit authority over the RevOps buildout so there's no ambiguity about who owns the data model. Watch for the warning signs that the sequence is failing: the CRO keeps asking for data that never materializes and doesn't move to fix that, activity increases but no shared definitions emerge, or every conversation is about coaching individual reps while the systemic pipeline questions go unanswered. Those are signs you have a leadership hire trying to substitute for an operations function that still doesn't exist. Cost-wise, be realistic that you're funding two things, not one — the CRO's fractional fee *and* the RevOps execution capacity they'll direct. Budgeting for the CRO alone and expecting them to magically produce clean operations for free is the single most common way this arrangement disappoints. If your budget only stretches to one, that's your signal to reconsider which gap is really the binding constraint, and often the honest answer is to build RevOps first and defer the CRO until the data can actually support one. ## What are the biggest risks of the CRO-first sequence, and how do you de-risk them? The headline risk is the mismatched hire: a strategy-only CRO parachuted onto a company with no operational floor. These CROs are excellent at the "what should our GTM motion be" conversation and helpless at "why does the CRM say we have $4M in pipeline when half of it is duplicate or dead." They'll produce a beautiful strategy deck and no durable machinery to execute it. De-risk this by screening explicitly for builders — ask for a specific story of a foundation they stood up from scratch — and by starting with a short paid trial or a 90-day term rather than an open-ended retainer. The second risk is the accountability gap that forms when nobody clearly owns the data. If the CRO assumes "someone" will handle CRM hygiene and reporting, and you assume the CRO will, the operational layer never gets built and both parties quietly lose faith. Close this by naming the RevOps buildout as an explicit CRO deliverable with a hire attached, not an ambient expectation. The third risk is premature optimization — a CRO who tries to install sophisticated multi-touch attribution or complex territory carving before the basics (stage definitions, a clean opportunity object) are solid. Foundations first; sophistication is earned once the base data is trustworthy. Across all three, the antidote is the same: make the RevOps foundation an explicit, milestoned, owned part of the engagement rather than an assumed byproduct of hiring someone senior. ## Related questions ### Is a fractional CRO worth it for a company under $2M in revenue? Usually not yet. Under roughly $2M, founder-led sales plus a strong RevOps contractor typically delivers more per dollar than a fractional CRO. The exception is a founder who is genuinely not a seller and needs commercial leadership to escape a growth ceiling. ### Can one person be both a fractional CRO and RevOps for a startup? Temporarily, yes — if they're specifically operations-literate. It's a viable bridge for cash-constrained companies, but it's a stopgap. As revenue grows, the strategic and operational workloads both expand past what one part-time person can cover, and the roles should split. ### How much does a fractional CRO cost compared to building RevOps first? Costs vary widely by market, scope, and seniority, so treat any single figure with caution. Directionally, a fractional CRO commands senior-executive day rates, while an early RevOps hire or contractor is materially cheaper. Get current quotes rather than relying on rules of thumb. ### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a RevOps consultant? A fractional CRO owns the revenue number and the commercial strategy across sales, marketing, and CS. A RevOps consultant builds and optimizes the operational infrastructure — data, process, tooling, reporting — that the CRO's decisions rely on. Different altitude, complementary work. ### Should the fractional CRO hire the RevOps person? Ideally the CRO defines the RevOps role and heavily influences the hire, since they know what the operational layer must produce. The founder should stay involved on budget and culture fit, but the CRO owning the spec keeps the two functions aligned from day one. ## FAQ **How long does it take a fractional CRO to build a RevOps foundation from scratch?** Plan for a full quarter to reach a trustworthy baseline — shared definitions, a clean CRM data model, and a forecast leadership believes. Deeper optimization continues well beyond 90 days, but the first quarter should produce a usable foundation. **Do I need a full-time CRO instead of a fractional one if I'm starting from zero?** Not necessarily. Starting from zero actually argues for fractional, because the early work is foundation-setting that doesn't require five days a week of a $300K executive. Scale up to full-time when the revenue org's complexity outgrows a part-time leader's bandwidth. **Can I skip the CRO and just hire RevOps if my founder is a strong seller?** Often yes. A founder who sells well and knows their GTM motion frequently just needs operational support to scale it. RevOps unblocks that founder at a fraction of a CRO's cost. Add the CRO later when the founder needs to step out of daily selling. **What CRM should be in place before hiring a fractional CRO?** Any mainstream CRM the CRO can standardize on — HubSpot and Salesforce are the common defaults. What matters far more than the specific tool is that the CRO has authority to fix its data model and stage definitions, because the tool is only as good as the discipline behind it. **How do I evaluate a fractional CRO when I have no data to judge them against?** Judge them on foundation deliverables, not revenue, in the first 90 days: did they produce adopted definitions, a trusted dashboard, a defensible forecast method, and a RevOps hire? Set these as explicit milestones up front, since you can't hold anyone to bookings that depend on infrastructure they're still building. **Will a fractional CRO commit long enough to build something durable?** A good one will, but you should structure for it. Use a defined term (a 90-day foundation phase is common), a written weekly commitment, and milestone-based continuation. The risk with fractional talent is divided attention, so make the engagement's scope and cadence explicit rather than assumed. **What if my fractional CRO says I need to build RevOps first?** That's usually a sign of a good hire, not a problem. It means they understand that their leverage depends on trustworthy signal. Let them scope and direct that buildout as part of the engagement — that's exactly the sequencing that makes the CRO-first approach work. **Is it a red flag if a fractional CRO wants to start by coaching reps?** When there's no operational foundation, yes. Rep coaching against untrustworthy pipeline data is activity without leverage. The first work should be diagnosis, definitions, and instrumentation. Coaching becomes valuable once you can actually see where deals break. ## Sources - [Harvard Business Review — Aligning Sales and Marketing Operations](https://hbr.org/2006/07/ending-the-war-between-sales-and-marketing) - [Gartner — Revenue Operations Research and Insights](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/topics/revenue-operations) - [Forrester — B2B Revenue Operations](https://www.forrester.com/research/revenue-operations/) - [McKinsey & Company — Growth, Marketing & Sales Insights](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights) - [SaaStr — Scaling Go-to-Market Leadership](https://www.saastr.com/) - [HubSpot Research — Sales and RevOps Benchmarks](https://www.hubspot.com/marketing-statistics) - [Salesforce — State of Sales Report](https://www.salesforce.com/resources/research-reports/state-of-sales/) - [Pavilion — Go-to-Market Leadership Community and Resources](https://www.joinpavilion.com/) ## Related on PULSE - [CRO vs. RevOps: Where the Scope Lines Actually Fall](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-vs-revops-scope) - [Structuring a Fractional CRO's First 90 Days](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-first-90-days) - [The RevOps Foundation Checklist for Early-Stage Companies](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-foundation-checklist) - [How to Know If You Have a Leadership Gap or an Operations Gap](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/leadership-vs-operations-gap) - [Building a Forecast Leadership Will Actually Trust](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/trustworthy-forecast-buildout)
